title: COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation in Middle Income Countries
screen_reason: This is primarily an NLP dataset-and-model paper (EMNLP 2023), which would normally fall under the 'detection/classifier work' exclusion. It is included because Section 5 applies the finished classifiers to the full collected corpus of 18.8 million geolocated tweets and Table 5 reports, per country and per year, the SHARE of COVID-19-vaccine-relevant tweets predicted to contain misinformation (Brazil 36.1%, Indonesia 19.4%, Nigeria 26.1%, overall 26.8%) with explicit numerators and denominators. That is a CONTENT share of items with a stated denominator. FLAG FOR ADJUDICATION: an adjudicator applying the classifier-paper exclusion strictly could screen this out; my reading is that the large-scale prevalence analysis (a substantive claim about three countries over three years, not a benchmark) makes it eligible.

estimates.measure_type: % of COVID-19-vaccine-relevant tweets predicted to contain COVID-19 vaccine misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 1,304,827 (36.1) of 3,619,091 COVID-19 vaccine relevant tweets [Table 5, Brazil country total]
estimates.denominator: 3,619,091 tweets predicted relevant to COVID-19 vaccines, out of 3,797,314 vaccine-relevant tweets, out of 5,524,644 geolocated Brazilian tweets collected with vaccine query terms (incl. Portuguese terms 'vacina', 'injecao', 'Ze Gotinha')
estimates.definition: Tweet predicted 'yes' by the XLM-R+_AUG misinformation classifier (Q3), trained on expert-annotated tweets coded for presence of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation, with themes drawn from Islam et al. (2021): vaccine development/availability/access, safety/efficacy/acceptance, infertility, political-economic motives, mandatory vaccine and ethics, vaccine reagents, vaccine morbidity/mortality, vaccine alternatives
estimates.misinfo_def: (Q3) presence of misinformation (yes/no/uncertain) ... Content deemed to be misinformation is labeled further for its themes based on a pre-identified list of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation themes (Islam et al., 2021) - the operational definitions live in the annotation codebook released on GitHub, not in the paper
estimates.ground_truth_detail: XLM-R+_AUG (multilingual XLM-RoBERTa with domain-specific further pre-training plus LLM text augmentation), macro F1 = 81.2 for Q3 misinformation; trained on tweets coded by two trained communication graduate students following a codebook, Gwet's inter-coder reliability 0.72 for the misinformation variable (mean .88 across all variables), with 'uncertain' tweets adjudicated by an expert public health panel. Classifier applied sequentially: vaccine relevance (Q1) -> non-COVID vaccine filter (Q2) -> misinformation (Q3).
estimates.moderator_quote: We collect all publicly available Twitter posts in Brazil, Indonesia, and Nigeria that contain vaccine-related terms from January 2020 to December 2022 (N = 18,809,231). ... Brandwatch enables us to scrape tweets specific to geolocations associated with the three focal countries. There are no language exclusions.
estimates.notes: Time series collapsed to the country total for 2020-2022 (the yearly cells are 26.8% in 2020, 25.1% in 2021, 40.3% in 2022, showing a steep rise). Denominator is the classifier-filtered COVID-vaccine-relevant subset, not all collected tweets - i.e. this is misinformation as a share of COVID-vaccine talk, not of all tweets. Two error sources compound: the Q1/Q2 relevance filters and the Q3 classifier (macro F1 81.2), and the authors themselves say model performance 'may still be suboptimal'. Per-country model performance differs with the share of English tweets (Brazil 77.16% English). Source quote is the pair of adjacent Table 5 cells in the row '# of Tweets Relevant to COVID-19 Vaccine Misinformation' - Brazil 2022 (1,040,556 = 40.3%) then Brazil country total (1,304,827 = 36.1%), which is the value used; the matching denominator cell one row above is '3,619,091 (95.3)'. The table is exploded cell-by-cell in the extracted text, so only the cell itself is a contiguous span.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Not extracted as a row: the pooled three-country figure, 2,474,046 of 9,236,334 COVID-19-vaccine-relevant tweets = 26.8%, because the protocol says to split by country; it is available if a pooled row is wanted. (2) Not extracted: the per-YEAR cells of Table 5 (Brazil 26.8 / 25.1 / 40.3; Indonesia 22.7 / 16.4 / 29.1; Nigeria 30.3 / 23.9 / 27.3 for 2020 / 2021 / 2022) - the time series was collapsed to the country total per the protocol. (3) DELIBERATELY NOT EXTRACTED, and the key judgement call here: the human-annotated prevalence in Table 1, Q3 'presence of misinformation' = 1,119 yes (37.2%), 1,596 no (53.0%), 296 uncertain (9.8%) of 3,011. This looks like a clean expert-coded prevalence but it is NOT one: the annotated set began as 5,500 tweets randomly sampled stratified by country, and then 'To balance the data for misinformation, we identify more tweets that contain misinformation, resulting in the final annotated dataset of N=5,952'. The denominator is therefore enriched with extra misinformation tweets by design and the 37.2% is upward-biased by an unstated amount. An adjudicator should not treat it as a prevalence estimate. (4) Not extracted: theme shares among misinformation tweets (Q4a 16.6%, Q4b 48.2%, Q4c 2.3%, Q4d 36.8%, Q4e 9.5%, Q4f 8.3%, Q4g 24.3%, Q4h 2.6% of the 1,119 misinformation tweets) - these are within-misinformation composition (within_misinfo_content territory) computed on the same enriched sample. (5) Not extracted: the relevance shares (51.3% of all collected tweets vaccine-relevant; 95.7% of those COVID-vaccine-relevant) - pipeline filters, not misinformation. (6) Not extracted: model performance (macro F1 81.2 for Q3, GPT-3 zero-shot 57.0) and the regression coefficients linking case growth to misinformation rates - not prevalence.

rob.design: Full keyword census of geolocated public tweets from Brazil, Indonesia and Nigeria, January 2020 - December 2022, N = 18,809,231, collected by hydrating Brandwatch-scraped IDs via the Twitter API with a vaccine query term list (no language exclusions; country-specific terms added; 'shot' included with noise limits). Annotation: Quantitative Content Analysis on 5,500 tweets randomly sampled stratified by country, coded by two trained communication graduate students against a released codebook for relevance (Q1), non-COVID vaccine mention (Q2), misinformation presence (Q3) and eight misinformation themes (Q4a-h); inter-coder reliability computed with Gwet's AC on 550 doubly coded posts - mean .88, relevance .98, non-COVID vaccine .97, misinformation .72, themes .87-.89; 'uncertain' misinformation cases adjudicated by an expert public health panel. The labelled set was then deliberately enriched with additional misinformation tweets to N = 5,952 for class balance. Models: XLM-RoBERTa with domain-specific further pre-training and LLM-based text augmentation; best macro F1 for misinformation = 81.2, applied sequentially to the full corpus. Stated limitations: the Nigerian Twitter ban (2021-2022) distorting Nigerian data, suboptimal model performance relying only on linguistic features, and 26 interpolated observations in the case-growth analysis.
rob.item6_quote: Two communication graduate students are trained as coders to examine the tweets for: (Q1) relevance to vaccine (yes/no), (Q2) mentions of specific non-COVID vaccine (such as the MMR vaccine) (yes/no), (Q3) presence of misinformation (yes/no/uncertain). Content deemed to be misinformation is labeled further for its themes based on a pre-identified list of COVID-19 vaccine misinformation themes (Islam et al., 2021)
